Anyway - enough of that. Yeah - I quite like the book, and I think Eliot Rosewater is one helluva good guy.

Matchmaking is neither consistent (otherwise many wouldn't be complaining) nor does it always match against similarly skilled opponents (again, if it did, many wouldn't find fault with it). It also doesn't always prioritise location of the players versus servers versus other players - which leads to high pings - and cannot guarantee a server that matches the exact specifications of a particular player that is looking for a specific gametype, map, playercount, location - and so on. Serverlists are old, yes, but there's a reason why they even existed in the first place - to allow players to pick which server they wanted to be on. Matchmaking does not allow a player full agency over what server they can or will join, as matchmaking is an automated system designed to take control away from the player in favour for simplifying the multiplayer experience.

The point is there is no reason why a game with a matchmaking system cannot also provide a serverlist feature for players who want to browse active hosts and pick what they want to join. You can't replace one with the other because they're completely different means to join multiplayer games. It's as if a fruit shop only sold oranges - and then bananas came out later on as an option. By your logic you'd throw out the oranges because now you have bananas - when in reality they both serve different purposes, and as a result should by all means both be an option at the fruit shop. They're complimentary. One is not better than the other in the sense of being an obvious upgrade as all that matchmaking does is search through a lump of online searching players, and throw together those that meet a statistical average in various small ad-hoc (typically peer-to-peer) parties. A serverlist displays active hosts and allows players to either look for matches based upon non-standard ways of play (that are otherwise buried beneath a whole slew of options or voting processes otherwise obscured by matchmaking), or, pick a location with the lowest ping.

All of this is coming from several years of game design and programming experience (both through College, University IT courses focusing on building and hosting servers coupled with complimentary game theory, and I am now currently at work on a commercial title with several colleagues that we aim for release in late 2017).
